findings.statement: CXCR2 tops the convergence ranking: up in UC in all five cohorts, meta-analysis log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264], and higher in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient (paired log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6972]). It has genetic and tractability support (CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists in clinical trials), but the bulk signal very likely reflects infiltrating neutrophils, so cell composition must be checked.

CXCL8, the neutrophil chemokine ligand of CXCR1 and CXCR2, is strongly and reproducibly up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.7037]) and is enriched in inflamed mucosa; it supports a neutrophil-recruitment axis (CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCR1, CXCR2 all up). Part of the signal comes from infiltrating myeloid cells, not only epithelium.

OSMR is up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=OSMR; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.042]) and local to inflamed mucosa (paired inflamed vs non-inflamed log2FC [gene=OSMR; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=0.8848]); it combines genetic association with an existing drug (vixarelimab) and fits the OSM/OSMR axis, expressed mainly by stromal cells.

HMGCS2, an epithelial ketogenesis and metabolism gene, is lost in UC in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845]). It is unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa versus control (log2FC [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=-0.0649]), so the loss marks local inflammation rather than the underlying disease. It is a biomarker, not a plausible target.

CHI3L1 has one of the largest and most reproducible increases (meta log2FC [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.7135]; up in all five cohorts). It is also modestly raised in non-inflamed MSCCR mucosa (log2FC [gene=CHI3L1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.8377]), so it reflects both local inflammation and a disease-level shift. It is a strong biomarker candidate with no approved drug.

JAK2 ranks high mainly through genetics and tractability; its expression change is small (meta log2FC [gene=JAK2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=0.872]). This is a modest, broadly replicated rise, not a strong transcriptional marker; the target case rests on genetics and existing JAK inhibitors, not on expression magnitude.

DUOX2 (with its maturation factor DUOXA2) is among the largest epithelial increases, up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.3213]) and clearly higher in inflamed mucosa of the same patient. It points to epithelial oxidative and antimicrobial stress and is a biomarker candidate, not a drugged target.

S100A8 (with S100A9, the calprotectin pair) is up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.6467]) and enriched in inflamed mucosa. This is largely a neutrophil and myeloid signal, consistent with calprotectin as a stool biomarker; the bulk increase may reflect infiltration rather than tissue-intrinsic change.

CD274 (PD-L1) is up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=CD274; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=1.887]) with genetic support; it looks like an interferon-driven, inflammation-induced regulatory feedback program, probably partly from immune cells, and is not an obvious inhibition target.

IDO1 is strongly up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.445]) and higher in inflamed mucosa, consistent with an interferon-gamma tryptophan-catabolism response. It has IDO1 inhibitors in oncology but no genetic support, and the immune-cell contribution is unresolved.

CLDN8, a tight-junction gene, is the strongest meta-analysis decrease (meta log2FC [gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.5181]; down in all five cohorts) and is lower in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa. Like other lost epithelial genes (SLC26A2, PCK1, AQP8), it indicates barrier and absorptive-epithelium loss, so it is a biomarker, not a target.

REG1A is strongly up and local to inflamed mucosa, but its replication is weaker than for the other top genes: it is not significant in the Leuven infliximab cohort GSE16879 (padj [gene=REG1A; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE16879; layer=rna; cohort=GSE16879; contrast=uc_vs_control; padj=0.132]), so four of five cohorts agree.

caveats: Heterogeneity across cohorts is high for most top genes (I2 near or above 0.9), so effect sizes differ between RNA-seq and microarrays; compare directions and significance, not magnitudes.
The four microarray cohorts have small control groups (12 to 21 controls, 18 in UNIFI).

Bulk expression cannot separate tissue-intrinsic change from neutrophil and myeloid infiltration; this affects CXCR1/2, CXCL8, S100A8/9, IDO1, CD274, MMPs and IL1B. Cell-composition analysis is needed.
Convergence scores for genetics, literature and tractability come from Open Targets and the knowledge graph, not from this expression data.
The data are cross-sectional biopsy transcriptomes; they do not show causality or therapeutic response.
